en: Wretched slave cast out by the people—
I shall pour out my contempt upon you.
Give me the falcon, and let me go!
Her tongue filled with venomous words,
While in her father's keeping
She sat giving birth to six children;
Black-faced source of calamity,
She grieved while wandering as a traveler.
Whenever she saw a man upon the road,
She ran with her skirts lifted.
I shall take that old woman.
An errand has come to my mind;
Give me my falcon, and I shall go!"
When Aichurok heard this,
The thought would not fit within her heart;
After hearing those deeply buried words,
Her tears scattered in ten directions:
"Enough, my lion-like lord!
Can a bridegroom be like you?
Can grieving Churok prosper
While burning like a cursed crow?
Ruined lord, may you come to no good!
I learned your coarseness long ago,
Yet I have honored the spirit
Of your father who departed this world!
Among the impetuous black Kyrgyz,
They said none was as coarse as you;
They said when frenzy seized you,
You were a rogue who slaughtered his Choro.
Among the gathered Argyn and Kyrgyz,
They said none was as harsh as you;
They said when anger truly seized you,
Beginning with his father Jakyp,
He was a rogue who slaughtered Abyke.
Among the six tribes of Kyrgyz and Argyn,
They said there was no fool like you.
I went about knowing you were a fool,
Yet I honored the looming spirit
Of your father who departed this world!
As though you had taken a wife,
As though you had placed a bridal scarf on my head,
As though you had entered into my delight,
As though you had lain in my embrace,
You went on roaring viciously
And pierced me to every bone.
I myself am broad-soled;
It is true that I am yellow.
It is also true that I grew old
At my father's home until childbearing age.
It is true I stripped the weariness
From my horse throughout the world;
It is true I went wandering,
Approaching all who appeared.
What you said is also true.
Yesterday, to the city of Temir Khan,
What sort of man were you, wandering away?
Saying, 'When will my companion return?'
What sort of woman was I, gazing down the road?
To the city of Kara Khan,
What sort of man were you, fleeing away?
Saying, 'When will my cherished one return?'
What sort of woman was I, grieving?
Was it you who lay in Bukhara,
Never turning aside or returning,
Saying, 'When will my champion return?'
Or I who kept mounting wheat-toothed horses,
And remained faithful without straying?
What sort of man were you,
Scattering toward your maternal uncle's city,
I have grown pale waiting for Dalai;
What am I, who has waited so long?!
Alas, because of your murderous fame,
I lived in fear of the ancestral spirits;
For many years I burned deliberately,
I knew your heart long ago,
And after all your promises and true words,
I kept pursuing what lay behind them!
Yesterday, when you did not come hunched over,
I put on my swan guise,
And at the shore of Ala-Köl
I cast down a walking mist;
The falcon in your hand
I swooped away and took.
The woman who knows not a bird's worth—
May her womanhood be damned;
I gave it knuckle meat from a yearling sheep,
And fed it until it was full;
God took your bird,
And it died of the flux.
I shall find you a bird like your bird;
My princely companion, hear my words.
That is what became of your bird.
It seems my name is woman,
And a woman's deed is maimed.
Yesterday, rejoicing after I took it,
I gave it too much forbidden meat
From a lean sheep;
It wasted away and died.
I shall find a bird like your bird;
That is what became of your bird!"
"Do not mock me, you bitch!
Give me my falcon and I shall leave;
If you sit there babbling,
I shall take you and make you pay!
I will accept no other bird,
I will not agree to what you say!
The proof that my bird was Akshunkar,
Its sure sign,
Is that for a wretch like you
Eighty maidens would be the fine.
Even if your father Akun offered in tribute
A hundred old women like you,
I would not accept them!"
As the prince stood there raging,
Chürök's anger rose:
"Alas, my prince, may ruin take you,
If we two cannot be reconciled!
Your falcon Akshunkar can be found again;
After your wretched, clamorous quarrel,
When can honor be found again?
The twelve joined hands as one,
And ten holy men gave their blessing;
Had the leopard now gone to the other world
Not been your father,
Had my father not driven livestock as in-laws,
Bowed in submission and eaten fat,
Started the great tumult,
Then cast me away saying he had given his daughter,
Had he not been my father,
Alas, because of your murderous fame,
And because of all the promises
Made by the blessed heroes,
I took you out of fear of this,
Though I did not like you as a husband!
Alas, because of your murderous fame,
How many men did I not test?
Though I tested him, why did I not marry
Kalcha there in Beijing!
I saw heroes in many lands;
Let me speak of the others.
If it is said again, it becomes another tale;
Let us not keep saying it again,
Saying, 'That is how she spoke.'
If it is told anew, it becomes a new tale;
Let us not ramble over it anew,
Saying, 'That is how she spoke then.'
Yesterday, that dear hair, thick as sedge,
When I pinned it atop my head,
My prince, despairing of you,
And wandered among the peoples,
I traveled through many lands.
Buyanbek of Muzburchak—
He too is no less than you,
No hero to be belittled!
Dwelling in Sary-Arka,
Called a formidable, weighty hero,
Kökchö's son Ümötöy—
He too is no less than you,
His valor is no lighter than yours!
Ürbü's son Zhosho—
In the land of Eki-Kemin
I saw him as I passed.
He too is no less than you,
His valor is no lighter than yours!
Dwelling in Kyzyl-Kyya,
Kyrym's son Muradyl,
Called a strong-backed hero—
He too is no less than you,
His valor is no lighter than yours!
Alas, because of your murderous fame,
How many did I test in passing?
Why did I test him yet not marry
Kalcha, the khan of Beijing!
With cotton sash and broad boots,
I saw with my own eyes at the ford
Kalcha standing there in splendor.
His beard was grizzled, it seems;
He was already growing old.
For the well-fed Kalcha,
His great boots jutting out,
His neck arched like a rooster's,
His stature proved fitting;
The soles of his boots
Were a full span broad.
Your father Manas
He was fit to strike down!
If only he were not so old,
The Chinese people's wide,
Red-mottled gown
Was what that hero would wear.
If only he were not Chinese,
That accursed Kalcha
Was a lion I would have married!
If you will not take me, do not, my murderer;
I shall go to Kongurbay.
If I do not die, I myself shall go,
Reach him, and marry him.
Karagul, chief of the herdsmen,
He too was one of the lions;
His valor is no less than yours,
No hero to be belittled!
I learned it from the transmitters,
And asked those who know.
I knew your temper long ago;
For the sake of your father gone to the other world,
I have honored your temper!
When driven to true fury,
They say, the madman slaughters his father;
However excellent you may be,
Among the six Kyrgyz tribes
They say there is no fool like you!
To a husband born unruly,
Let me stand yearning and speak:
If you will not take me, do not, my murderer;
I too shall find my equal and leave!"
Saying this and tormenting him, Aychürök
Was deeply hurt by the hero,
And sobbed and wept bitterly.
Unable to draw back the mucus from her nose,
Unable to wipe the tears from her eyes—
Whose first ancestor was Tügöl Khan,
Whose root was blessed by Khydyr,
Descendant of the deathless one,
Growing stronger whenever one died,
Descendant of a sovereign hero:
"I know you, wretch;
I know the waist you girded,
I know, Aychürök,
Your Chinese husband in Beijing!
I shall break your back,
I shall cool your breath,
I shall drive out of you
All your far-flung bluster—
The husbands you sought and chose,
Chynkozho and Toltoy!
I shall show the strength of my arm,
And begin many a tumult!
I shall bring the end of the age,
And take warrior Toltoy!
Luckless woman who went seeking men,
I shall take you and make you pay.
Come here without delay;
Give me the falcon and I shall leave!"
Your murderer grew furious
And now stood hunched over.
From father back to forefather,
Descendant of black-hearted men—
"He will leave without taking me," she thought,
And God now struck Chürök.
Your dear sister-in-law wailed,
Offended by her murderer.
Weeping hard and sobbing,
She reeled, her knees giving way,
Despairing of her destroyer.
In crimson gown, with a moonlike waist,
Your graceful sister-in-law,
